newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit reaches landmark budget discipline pact.
newsitem.headline: EU summit reaches landmark budget discipline pact.

text.p: After a hard-fought Franco-German battle, European Union leaders agreed on a landmark pact on budget discipline on Friday that takes the 15-nation bloc a major step closer to a single currency in 1999.
On the day that European monetary authorities unveiled the future euro banknotes, leaders approved strict limits on the budget deficits of countries that join monetary union.
But in deference to France and other defenders of national sovereignty, they allowed for a political judgment on whether to levy fines on those who overspend.

"This is a victory for Europe. This is a victory for the euro," European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy exulted, saying approval of a "Stability and Growth Pact" had sent the right signal to financial markets.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who had pressed for the strictest possible rules of fiscal orthodoxy, told a news conference he was satisfied with the outcome, even though it fell short of the binding, automatic sanctions Bonn had sought.
"The stability pact is a credible signal that the euro will be a hard currency," he said. Asked whether the euro would be as hard as the deutschemark, Waigel said "Jawohl!" (Yes indeed).

Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, who chaired the talks that crafted the compromise, said there had been "philosophical and ideological debate about the nature of sovereignty", which he joked did not come easily to finance ministers.

Quinn said the summit had also approved the legal basis of the euro and a mechanism linking it to the currencies of member states that do not immediately join monetary union. That is meant to prevent competitive devaluations that distort trade.
The summit formally confirmed Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg as head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) from next July, succeeding Belgian Alexandre Lamfalussy.
But French President Jacques Chirac said that did not mean Duisenberg would automatically head the future European central bank, which will control monetary policy for the euro.
Symbolically, the EMI unveiled the first euro banknotes in Dublin on Friday, giving millions of Europeans a first glimpse of the currency that will enter their pockets in 2002.

The notes avoid national symbols, landmarks or figures, featuring generic European architectural designs and bridges instead. But they leave space for each member state to put a national symbol if the EU so decides.

When the summit opened on Friday morning, Germany, whose citizens are wary of giving up the hard deutschemark for the untried euro, held out for tighter rules defining when countries could be exempted from fines for overspending.
Ministers said Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, who is also his country's finance minister, played the key role in bridging the Franco-German differences.

In the end, leaders agreed that countries would be exempted from penalties for running a deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product if their economies shrank by more than two percent in a year.
But any fine would be subject to a political judgment if there was a recession of more than 0.75 percent of GDP.

The European Commission launched a publicity campaign to ease public acceptance of the new currency earlier this week, unveiling a dollar-style symbol -- a "c" with two horizantal dashes through it -- which it is to represent the euro.

While ministers haggled behind the scenes on the final wording of the stability pact, the leaders endured a lecture by British Prime Minister John Major on how they should copy Britain's sweeping labour market deregulation to create jobs.
"Nobody reacted," said one minister at the meeting. "It was a monologue. There was no dialogue."

The growing sense of inevitability about the single currency, despite the stability pact wrangle, made this an uncomfortable summit for Major, whose Conservative government, torn over European policy, lost its parliamentary majority on Thursday when the opposition Labour party won a by-election.
Facing a general election by May, Major is under pressure from within his party to rule out Britain joining the euro.

After completing their euro agreement, the leaders moved on to the other main agenda item -- a drive to reform EU institutions in preparation for admitting former communist central European countries from around the year 2000.

The Irish presidency of the EU has produced a report to increase cooperation in foreign, defence, interior and justice affairs but it has left aside for now the issue of greater majority voting most sensitive to Britain.

France and Germany put forward their own proposals for greater integration on Monday, saying it was vital to give the slow-moving negotiations new momentum if a substantial reform is to be achieved by the deadline of next June in Amsterdam.
